newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli closure hurts Bethlehem tourism.
newsitem.headline: Israeli closure hurts Bethlehem tourism.

text.p: Struggling to save his business from collapse, Palestinian Tawfiq Lama waited with a fleet of empty taxis as tourists walked across an Israeli army checkpoint on their way to visit the birthplace of Jesus Christ.

Facing growing losses after a week-long Israeli ban on the entry of tourist buses from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, the 33-year-old souvenir shop owner has been contracting private taxis to pick up visitors from the Israeli checkpoint and take them to visit holy sites and then ferry them to his store.

"This is costing me a lot of money. But it is the only way to bring in tourists," Lama said. He said less than 20 percent of the normal number of tourists visiting Bethlehem at this time of the year have entered the city.
"Nobody wants to walk across the checkpoint. They become afraid when they are told that they have to leave their buses behind and walk," he said.
Israel sealed off the Palestinian self-rule areas following gunbattles and clashes last month, barring its citizens from travel to the West Bank.
The Israeli army says the closure, which includes barring tourist buses, was imposed for security reasons.
But the Israeli measure has infuriated Palestinians, who view the Israeli measure as collective punishment.

The Palestinian Authority said on Tuesday it was barring Palestinians from bringing in tourists in private vehicles, demanding instead that Israel lift the bus ban. But the order was not strictly enforced and some tourists still entered Bethlehem in convoys after crossing the checkpoint on foot.
The Palestinian Ministry of Economy and Trade said Israeli restrictions on the West Bank and Gaza Strip have raised daily Palestinian losses to about $10 million from $6 million before the violence.
Israel and Jordan reported a drop in the number of tourists arriving since the violence which claimed the lives of 59 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.

But the Palestinian self-rule areas, already reeling from restrictions imposed following a spate of Islamic suicide bombings in February and March, have suffered most. Palestinian tourism officials estimate that tourism revenues amount to about $170 million a year.

In Bethlehem, the biggest tourist-drawing town under Palestinian self-rule, the ban has prompted many groups to cancel hotel reservations and discouraged many already in Israel from travelling to the city.
The Palestinian Ministry of Tourism gave no figures for the losses. But officials said souvenir shops, restaurants and hotels had all been hurt badly by the closure.
"The Palestinian tourist sector has been paralysed," said Bajes Ismael, director-general of the Palestinian Tourism Ministry.
Doris Awad, in charge of the reception and reservations at the 160-room Bethlehem hotel, said the Israeli closure ruined what could have been the tourism high season in the city.
She said three tourist groups occupying 130 rooms in the hotel checked out three days ahead of schedule because of the closure and more had been calling to cancel.

"We were expecting an over-booking for the month of October. But as of now, we have about 40 percent booking and even those are already considering cancelling," she said. "This would have been our peak season. But it all has been ruined."
At Manger square, usually packed with buses, only a few tourists waited for rides to take them back to Israel. Private cars were parked in the lot reserved for tourist buses.

"As far as I recall, this is the first time in 30 years that Israel imposed such stringent measures on the entry of tourists," said Jiryes Freij, who owns a souvenir shop on Manger square. "We have not had one customer today."
